oneLineAnswer: A common medicine for everyday pain and fever; too much at once harms the liver.
whatItIs: Paracetamol is the name used in many countries for the medicine known in the United States as acetaminophen. It is a pain reliever and fever reducer that you take by mouth. It comes as tablets, capsules, liquids, powders and suppositories. It is a different medicine from anti-inflammatory painkillers called NSAIDs, such as ibuprofen.
whatItDoes: It eases everyday pain, such as headaches, sore muscles, toothache and period cramps.
It also lowers fever for a while.
Labels sum it up as a pain reliever and fever reducer.
The exact way it works is not established, a US label says.
It seems to act mainly in the brain and spinal cord.
howPeopleUseIt: People take it for common problems such as headaches, colds, backache and muscle aches.
It is sold as tablets, capsules, liquids, powders and suppositories.
It is also an ingredient in hundreds of combination medicines, including cold, cough, allergy and sleep products.
Brand names differ by country; well known ones include Tylenol and Panadol.
FDA warns that using two products that both contain it can add up to an accidental overdose.

commonSideEffects: The most common side effects recorded in trials of injected acetaminophen were nausea, vomiting, headache and insomnia.
Those trials used an injected form, so they do not describe what tablets or liquids feel like.
seriousSigns: Too much can damage the liver; FDA says this can lead to liver failure and death.
Your liver processes the drug, and a large amount at once overloads that process, FDA says.
Signs of liver disease FDA lists include yellow skin and eyes, dark urine, pale stools, nausea and vomiting.
Rare but serious skin reactions can happen, with reddening, rash, blisters or peeling of the upper skin.
FDA says a serious skin reaction can appear even if earlier use caused no problem.
whoShouldAvoid: FDA says to ask a health professional before use if you have liver disease.
A US prescription label lists severe liver disease as a reason not to use the medicine.
Ask a doctor first if you are allergic to acetaminophen or to an ingredient in the product.
FDA says people who had a serious skin reaction to it should not take it again.
FDA warns that three or more alcoholic drinks a day raises the risk of liver damage.
FDA says not to give an adult product to a child under 12.

interactions: FDA says to avoid using more than one product that contains acetaminophen at the same time.
FDA also states the 24-hour total from all sources should not go above 4,000 mg.
That limit is for adults and children 12 and older.
Labels say to ask a doctor or pharmacist before use if you take warfarin, a blood-thinning drug.
Short forms such as APAP, acetamin and acetam can hide acetaminophen on a prescription label.
pregnancyAndChildren: FDA says it has not found clear evidence that appropriate use in pregnancy causes problems for the baby. It still advises talking to a health professional first. For children, FDA says to read the label. It also says to use the measuring device sold with a liquid product, not a kitchen spoon. FDA says never to give an adult product to a child under 12.
whatWeDoNotKnow: This record gives no dosing instructions and is not medical advice.
The exact way paracetamol eases pain and fever is still not established, a US label says.
Everyday side effects for tablets and liquids are not described on the public pages fetched.
The side effect list here comes from trials of an injected form.
FDA says it continues to watch pain medicine use in pregnancy, so that evidence is not settled.
How often serious harm happens in ordinary use is not stated on the pages fetched.
